title: Book IV: Three Love Problems — Chapter XXXVII
paragraphs:
Thrice happy she that is so well assured
Unto herself and settled so in heart
That neither will for better be allured
Ne fears to worse with any chance to start,
But like a steddy ship doth strongly part
The raging waves and keeps her course aright;
Ne aught for tempest doth from it depart,
Ne aught for fairer weather’s false delight.
Such self-assurance need not fear the spight
Of grudging foes; ne favour seek of friends;
But in the stay of her own stedfast might
Neither to one herself nor other bends.
Most happy she that most assured doth rest,
But he most happy who such one loves best.
—SPENSER.

Mr. Vincy’s uncertainty about whether a general election or the end of the world was approaching only faintly represented the confusion of provincial opinion. George IV was dead, Parliament dissolved, Wellington and Peel widely disparaged, and the new King apologetic. By the glowworm light available in country towns, how could people distinguish their own thoughts amid it all? A Tory government was passing Liberal measures; Tory peers and voters wanted to elect Liberals rather than supporters of ministers they considered traitors. Demands for remedies seemed mysteriously remote from private interests, and became suspect when disagreeable neighbors supported them. Middlemarch newspaper buyers occupied a peculiar position. During the agitation over the Catholic Question, many had stopped buying the “Pioneer,” a paper bearing a motto from Charles James Fox and marching at the head of progress. It had sided with Peel on the Catholics, staining its Liberalism by tolerating Jesuitry and Baal. Yet the “Trumpet” did not satisfy them either. After its blasts against Rome, and amid a general limpness of public opinion, when nobody knew who would support whom, its notes had grown feeble.

According to a notable article in the “Pioneer,” the country’s urgent needs might now properly overcome any reluctance to enter public life in men whose long experience had given their minds breadth as well as concentration, firm judgment as well as tolerance, dispassion as well as energy. In other words, all those qualities which humanity’s melancholy experience finds least willing to live together.

Mr. Hackbutt’s fluent conversation was circulating more widely than usual just then, with considerable uncertainty about where it would finally flow. In Mr. Hawley’s office he was heard to declare that the article “emanated” from Brooke of Tipton, who had secretly purchased the “Pioneer” several months earlier.

“Trouble brewing, then?” said Mr. Hawley. “After drifting about like a stray tortoise, he’s taken it into his head to become popular. The worse for him. I’ve been watching him for some time. We’ll give him a thorough ducking. He’s a damned bad landlord. What’s an old county gentleman doing courting a vulgar set of dark-blue freemen? As for his newspaper, I only hope he’ll write it himself. We could afford to pay him for that.”

“I’m told he’s hired a remarkably brilliant young man as editor, someone capable of writing leading articles in the finest style, equal to anything in the London papers. And he intends to take a very elevated line on Reform.”
“Let Brooke reform his rent roll. He’s a damned old miser, and every building on his estate is falling apart. I suppose this young fellow is some disreputable London adventurer.”
“His name is Ladislaw. They say he’s of foreign descent.”
“I recognize the breed,” Mr. Hawley replied. “Some sort of agent. He’ll start by flourishing the Rights of Man and finish by murdering a girl. That’s their way.”

“You must admit there are abuses, Hawley,” said Mr. Hackbutt, anticipating a political disagreement with his family lawyer. “I’d never support extreme opinions. My own position is Huskisson’s, in fact. But I can’t ignore the consideration that large towns without representation—”

“Damn the large towns!” Mr. Hawley had no patience for exposition. “I know rather too much about Middlemarch elections. Abolish every pocket borough tomorrow and enfranchise every mushroom town in the kingdom; all you’ll do is make getting into Parliament more expensive. I rely on facts.”

Mr. Hawley resented both the idea of an agent editing the “Pioneer” and Brooke’s entry into active politics, as though a tortoise of wandering interests had thrust out its little head in ambition and reared up. Yet some of Mr. Brooke’s family resented it still more. The truth had gradually leaked out, like the discovery that your neighbor has established an offensive manufacture whose odors you must permanently endure without legal recourse. The “Pioneer” had been bought secretly before Will Ladislaw arrived. The awaited opportunity came when its owner proved willing to part with valuable property that yielded no profit. In the time since Mr. Brooke had written his invitation to Will, the germ of an ambition to bring his mind to bear on the wider world had been growing in secret. It had existed since his youth, but until now something had always impeded it.

His pleasure in his guest, greater even than expected, did much to encourage this growth. Will not only knew his way around all those artistic and literary subjects Mr. Brooke had once explored. He was also extraordinarily quick at grasping the political situation and treating it in the broad-minded spirit which, when supported by a good memory, lends itself to apt quotation and an effective handling of the whole.

“He strikes me as a sort of Shelley, you know,” Mr. Brooke took an opportunity to tell Mr. Casaubon, intending to please him. “Nothing objectionable, I don’t mean—loose morals, atheism, any of that, you know. I’m certain Ladislaw’s feelings are sound in every respect. We talked a great deal last night, as it happens. But he has that same enthusiasm for liberty, freedom, emancipation. Excellent things when guided—properly guided, you know. I think I can set him on the right course. And it’s especially gratifying that he’s your relative, Casaubon.”

If “the right course” meant anything more definite than the rest of this speech, Mr. Casaubon silently hoped it meant employment a long way from Lowick. He had disliked Will while supporting him, and disliked him still more now that Will had refused support. So it goes with those of us whose disposition contains an uneasy jealousy. If our own talents chiefly involve burrowing, we suspect that our honey-sipping cousin, against whom we have serious objections, secretly despises us. Anyone admiring him indirectly criticizes us. Our scrupulous sense of right keeps us above the meanness of harming him. Instead, we actively confer benefits to satisfy every claim he has on us. Writing him checks establishes a superiority he must acknowledge, and this softens our bitterness. Now, abruptly and capriciously, Mr. Casaubon had lost that superiority, except as a memory. His hostility toward Will arose from something deeper than an aging husband’s ordinary jealousy. It had grown out of lifelong pretensions and dissatisfactions. But Dorothea’s presence—Dorothea as a young wife who had herself shown an offensive capacity for criticism—inevitably focused an uneasiness that had once been diffuse.

Will Ladislaw, meanwhile, felt his dislike growing at gratitude’s expense, and argued extensively with himself to justify it. Casaubon hated him; he knew that perfectly. The instant he entered, he could detect bitterness around the mouth and venom in the glance, enough almost to justify open war despite past kindness. He owed Casaubon much for the past, but really, marrying this particular wife canceled the debt. Ought gratitude for kindness to oneself to outweigh anger at a wrong done to someone else? Casaubon had wronged Dorothea by marrying her. A man had a duty to know himself better. If he chose to grow gray gnawing bones in a cave, he had no right to entice a girl into sharing it. “The most horrible sacrifice of a virgin,” Will called it. He pictured Dorothea’s secret suffering as though composing a lament for a tragic chorus. But he would never lose sight of her. He would protect her; if he sacrificed everything else, he would still protect her. She should know she had one slave in the world. Will possessed what Sir Thomas Browne called a “passionate prodigality” in his declarations, to himself as well as to others. The plain truth was that nothing attracted him then so powerfully as Dorothea’s presence.

Formal invitations had been absent, however: Will had never been asked to Lowick. Mr. Brooke, sure he was doing all the agreeable things poor, absorbed Casaubon forgot to do, had arranged several times to bring Ladislaw there. Meanwhile he introduced him everywhere else whenever possible as “a young relative of Casaubon’s.” Will had not seen Dorothea alone. Even so, their meetings restored her old sense of youthful companionship with someone cleverer than herself who nevertheless seemed willing to be influenced by her. Before marriage, poor Dorothea had seldom found much space in other people’s minds for what she most wanted to say. And her husband’s superior instruction, as we know, had brought her less pleasure than expected. When she spoke to Mr. Casaubon with eager interest, he listened patiently, as though she were quoting an elementary Delectus passage he had known since childhood. Sometimes he curtly named ancient sects or individuals who had held similar ideas, implying an excessive supply of that commodity already. Sometimes he told her she was mistaken and repeated the assertion her remark had challenged.

Will Ladislaw, however, always appeared to discover more in her words than she did herself. Dorothea had little vanity, but she had a passionate woman’s need to exercise a kindly influence by making another soul happy. The mere possibility of seeing Will now and then was therefore like a little window opened in her prison wall, offering a glimpse of sunlit air. That pleasure began to overcome her first alarm about what her husband might think of Will’s arrival as her uncle’s guest. Mr. Casaubon had said nothing on that subject.

Will wanted a private conversation with Dorothea and grew impatient with circumstances moving so slowly. Dante and Beatrice, Petrarch and Laura, might have enjoyed little earthly conversation, but time changes the proportions of things. In later ages fewer sonnets and more conversation are preferable. Necessity justified a scheme, though fear of offending Dorothea limited his ingenuity. At last he discovered a wish to sketch a particular view at Lowick. One morning, when Mr. Brooke had to take the Lowick road toward the county town, Will asked to be dropped there with sketchbook and folding stool. Without announcing himself at the manor, he chose a drawing position from which he must see Dorothea if she came out. He knew she generally walked for an hour each morning.

The weather defeated his plan. Clouds assembled with treacherous speed, rain fell, and Will had to shelter in the house. Relying on his family connection, he meant to go into the drawing room and wait without being announced. Seeing his old acquaintance, the butler, in the hall, he said, “Don’t announce me, Pratt. I’ll wait until lunch. I know Mr. Casaubon dislikes being interrupted in the library.”

“The master’s out, sir. Only Mrs. Casaubon’s in the library. I’d better let her know you’ve come.” Pratt was a red-cheeked man who enjoyed lively chats with Tantripp and often agreed that Madam must find life dull.
“Oh, all right. This wretched rain has stopped me drawing,” Will replied. He was so happy that pretending indifference came delightfully easily.
A minute later he stood in the library, and Dorothea greeted him with her sweet, unaffected smile.

“Mr. Casaubon has gone to the Archdeacon’s,” she said immediately. “I’m not sure he’ll return much before dinner. He didn’t know how long he’d be away. Did you need to discuss something particular with him?”
“No, I came to draw, but the rain drove me indoors. Otherwise I wouldn’t have interrupted you yet. I thought Mr. Casaubon was here, and I know he dislikes interruptions at this time of day.”
“Then I owe the rain a debt. I’m so pleased to see you.” These ordinary words had the unguarded sincerity of an unhappy schoolchild receiving a visitor.

“Actually, I came hoping to see you alone,” Will admitted, mysteriously compelled to match her simplicity. He could not stop to ask himself why he should not. “I wanted us to talk as we did in Rome. Having other people present always changes things.”

“Yes,” Dorothea agreed in her clear, full voice. “Please sit down.” She sat on a dark ottoman against a background of brown books. In her plain dress of thin white wool, wearing no ornament except her wedding ring, she seemed vowed to be unlike all other women. Will sat opposite, two yards away. Light fell on his bright curls and fine, slightly petulant profile, with its defiant curves of chin and lip. They looked at each other like two flowers that had opened just then and there. For the moment Dorothea forgot her husband’s inexplicable irritation with Will. To speak without fear to the one person she had found receptive was fresh water to thirsty lips. Looking backward through unhappiness, she magnified a former comfort.
“I’ve often wished we could talk again,” she said at once. “It’s strange to remember how much I told you.”

“I remember every word,” Will replied. His soul held an inexpressible contentment at being with someone worthy of perfect love. I think his feelings then were perfect too. We mortals have divine moments, when love finds satisfaction in the completeness of the person loved.

“Since Rome, I’ve tried to learn a great deal,” Dorothea said. “I can read a little Latin, and I’m starting to understand a very little Greek. I’m more useful to Mr. Casaubon now. I can look up references and spare his eyes in various ways. But scholarship is terribly difficult. People seem to exhaust themselves on the journey toward great thoughts, and when they reach them they’re too tired to enjoy them.”

“Anyone capable of great thoughts generally catches up with them before becoming decrepit,” Will answered with uncontrollable quickness. Certain sensitivities made Dorothea as quick as he was, however. Seeing her expression change, he immediately added, “Still, it’s certainly true that even the finest minds sometimes strain themselves too far in developing their ideas.”

“You’re correcting me,” said Dorothea. “I didn’t put it well. I meant that people with great thoughts wear themselves out working them through. I used to feel for them even as a little girl. I always thought the best use I could make of my life would be to help someone doing great work, and lighten his burden.”

She had drifted into this piece of personal history without feeling she was revealing a secret. Yet nothing she had ever told Will illuminated her marriage so clearly. He refrained from shrugging. Denied that muscular release, his thoughts turned all the more irritably to beautiful lips kissing holy skulls and other hollow things enshrined by the Church. He also had to keep those thoughts out of his speech.

“But you could easily help too much,” he said, “and exhaust yourself. Aren’t you indoors too much? You’re already paler. A secretary would be better for Mr. Casaubon. He could easily find a man to do half his work. That would spare him more effectively, and leave you to help in less demanding ways.”

“How can you suggest that?” Dorothea protested earnestly. “Helping him with his work is my only happiness. What else could I do? There’s no useful work for me in Lowick. All I want is to help him more. Besides, he objects to a secretary. Please don’t suggest it again.”
“Certainly I won’t, now that I understand your feelings. But both Mr. Brooke and Sir James Chettam have said they wish he had one.”

“Yes, but they don’t understand. They want me to spend hours riding, redesign the garden, build conservatories, anything to fill my time. I thought you’d understand that the mind needs other things,” she added with some impatience. “And Mr. Casaubon can’t bear the subject of a secretary.”
“You can excuse my mistake,” Will replied. “He used to speak as if he looked forward to having one. In fact, he once suggested the position to me. But I turned out to be—not good enough for it.”
Trying to find in this an explanation that excused her husband’s obvious aversion, Dorothea smiled playfully. “You weren’t a sufficiently steady worker.”

“No,” Will agreed, tossing his head back like a spirited horse. Then the old irritable demon urged him to pinch another piece from the fragile moth wings of poor Mr. Casaubon’s glory. “And I’ve since realized he doesn’t want anyone examining his work closely enough to know exactly what he’s doing. He’s too doubtful, too unsure of himself. I may be worth very little, but he dislikes me because I disagree with him.”

Will did intend always to behave generously. But tongues are little triggers, usually pulled before general intentions can be brought into play. It was unbearable to leave Dorothea without a fair explanation of Casaubon’s dislike. Once he had spoken, though, he worried a little about how she would take it.

Dorothea remained unexpectedly quiet. She did not respond with instant indignation as she had on a similar occasion in Rome. The reason lay deep. She had stopped fighting against seeing the facts and was learning to see them clearly. Looking steadily now at her husband’s failure, and still more at his possible awareness of it, she seemed to see the one path on which duty could become tenderness. She might have rebuked Will’s frankness more sharply had her husband’s dislike not already commended him to her mercy. Until she understood its grounds better, that dislike must seem harsh.

She did not answer immediately. After gazing down thoughtfully, she said with some earnestness, “Whatever his feelings, Mr. Casaubon has overcome them in his behavior toward you. That deserves admiration.”

“Yes, he has recognized what justice requires within a family. Disinheriting my grandmother for what they called a _mesalliance_ was disgraceful. The only charge against her husband was that he was a Polish refugee who earned a living by teaching.”
“I wish I knew her whole story!” Dorothea exclaimed. “How did she manage the change from wealth to poverty? I wonder whether she was happy with her husband! Can you tell me much about them?”

“Very little. My grandfather was a patriot, a clever man, spoke several languages, had musical ability, taught all sorts of things to earn his bread. They both died fairly young. And apart from what my mother told me, I knew little of my father. He inherited the musical gifts. I remember his slow walk, his long, thin hands. One day stays in my mind: he was lying ill, and I was desperately hungry, with only a little piece of bread.”

“How unlike my own life!” Dorothea said with intense interest, clasping her hands in her lap. “I’ve always had too much of everything. But explain it to me. Mr. Casaubon can’t have known about you then.”

“No. But my father contacted him, and that was the last day I went hungry. Father died soon afterward, and my mother and I were well provided for. Mr. Casaubon always specifically acknowledged a duty toward us because of the cruel injustice done to his mother’s sister. But you already know all this.”

Deep down, Will knew he wanted to impress something on Dorothea that was rather new even in his own account of events: Mr. Casaubon had only ever been paying a debt to him. Will was much too decent to feel comfortable with ingratitude. Once gratitude becomes an issue to reason over, however, many ways of escaping its bonds present themselves.

“No,” Dorothea replied. “Mr. Casaubon has never liked dwelling on his own good deeds.” She did not feel that her husband’s conduct had been diminished. But this conception of what justice had required him to do for Will took a powerful hold on her. After a pause she added, “He never told me he supported your mother. Is she alive?”

“No. She died in an accident—a fall—four years ago. Oddly enough, she had run away from her family too, though not because of her husband. She would tell me nothing about them except that she left to earn her own living. She went on the stage, in fact. She had dark eyes and tight curls and never seemed to grow older. So you see, I have rebellious blood on both sides.” Will ended with a bright smile at Dorothea. She was still gazing ahead with grave absorption, like a child watching her first play.

Then she smiled too. “That’s your excuse, I suppose, for your own rebelliousness—against Mr. Casaubon’s wishes, I mean. Remember, you haven’t followed the course he thought best for you. If he dislikes you—you mentioned dislike earlier—or rather, if he’s shown any unhappy feeling toward you, you must remember how sensitive the strain of study has made him. Perhaps,” she went on in a pleading voice, “my uncle hasn’t told you how seriously ill he was. Those of us who are well, who can bear things, would be petty to dwell on little offenses from people carrying such heavy troubles.”

“You show me a better way,” Will said. “I won’t complain about that again.” His gentleness came from an inexpressible satisfaction at recognizing something Dorothea barely knew herself: she was retreating into the distance of pure pity and loyalty toward her husband. Will was ready to worship that pity and loyalty if she would let him join her in expressing them. “I’ve certainly been difficult at times,” he continued. “But if I can help it, I’ll never again say or do anything you’d disapprove of.”

“That’s very kind,” Dorothea said, smiling openly again. “Then I’ll have a little kingdom where I can make laws. But I suppose you’ll soon leave and escape my rule. You’ll tire of the Grange before long.”

“That’s something I wanted to discuss with you—one reason I hoped to see you alone. Mr. Brooke has suggested I stay nearby. He’s bought a Middlemarch newspaper and wants me to run it and assist him in other matters.”
“Wouldn’t that mean giving up better prospects?” Dorothea asked.

“Possibly. But people have always criticized me for dreaming of prospects instead of settling to work. Here’s an actual offer. If you don’t want me to accept, I won’t. Otherwise I’d prefer staying in this part of the country to leaving. There’s nobody elsewhere I belong to.”
“I’d very much like you to stay,” Dorothea answered immediately, with the same ready simplicity she had shown in Rome. At that instant she could think of no possible reason not to say it.
“Then stay I _will_,” said Ladislaw, tossing back his head. He stood and walked toward the window as if checking whether the rain had stopped.

A moment later, however, Dorothea fell into a habit growing stronger every day: remembering that her husband felt differently. She blushed deeply, doubly embarrassed at having expressed a wish that might oppose his, and at needing to reveal that disagreement to Will. His turned back made it easier for her to speak—

“But my opinion hardly matters in a question like this. You should take Mr. Casaubon’s advice. I was thinking only of my feelings, which have nothing to do with the actual issue. It occurs to me now that he might find the proposal unwise. Could you wait and discuss it with him?”

“I can’t stay today,” Will said, inwardly scorched by the possibility of Mr. Casaubon’s arrival. “The rain has stopped entirely. I told Mr. Brooke not to collect me. I’d rather walk the five miles. I’ll cross Halsell Common and watch the light on the wet grass. I enjoy that.”

He hurried over to shake hands, desperately wanting to say, “Don’t mention this to Mr. Casaubon,” but unable to risk it. No, he could not say such a thing. Asking her to be less open and straightforward would be like breathing on crystal through which you wanted to see the light. There was also the other great fear: that he himself might lose his brightness in her eyes, and remain forever without it.

“I wish you could have stayed,” Dorothea said with a faint sadness, rising and offering her hand. She too had an unspoken thought. Will certainly ought to consult Mr. Casaubon’s wishes without delay, but urging him might seem too dictatorial.

They therefore said only goodbye. Will left across the fields to avoid any chance of meeting Mr. Casaubon’s carriage, which in fact did not reach the gate until four. That was an awkward time to return. It was too early to relieve his weariness with the moral support of dressing for dinner, yet too late to strip his mind of the day’s empty ceremonies and business and plunge properly into serious study. Usually at such times he settled into a library armchair, closed his eyes, and let Dorothea read the London papers aloud. Today he declined, saying he had already been subjected to too many public details. But when she asked about his tiredness, he answered more cheerfully than usual. Then, with the laborious formality that never left him, even without waistcoat or cravat, he added—

“Today I enjoyed meeting my old acquaintance Dr. Spanning, and receiving praise from someone himself deserving of praise. He spoke most generously of my recent treatise on the Egyptian Mysteries. Indeed, his terms were such that modesty prevents my repeating them.” As he said this last part, Mr. Casaubon leaned over the arm of his chair and bobbed his head, apparently finding a muscular release in place of the repetition propriety forbade.
“I’m so glad you had that pleasure,” Dorothea said, delighted that he seemed less weary than usual at this hour. “Before you returned, I’d been sorry you happened to be out today.”
“Why, my dear?” Mr. Casaubon asked, leaning back again.

“Mr. Ladislaw came. He told me about a proposal Uncle has made, and I’d like to hear what you think.” She felt this really did concern her husband. Inexperienced as she was, she vaguely sensed that the position offered to Will did not fit his family connections. Certainly Mr. Casaubon deserved to be consulted. He said nothing, merely bowing.
“You know how many plans dear Uncle has. Apparently he’s bought one of the Middlemarch newspapers. He’s asked Mr. Ladislaw to remain nearby and manage it, as well as help him in other ways.”
She watched her husband while speaking. At first he blinked, then closed his eyes as though resting them, while his lips tightened. After a short pause, she asked rather timidly, “What do you think?”

“Did Mr. Ladislaw visit expressly to seek my opinion?” Mr. Casaubon’s eyes opened narrowly, fixing her with a look as sharp as a knife. His question touched a point on which she truly felt uneasy. But her face merely grew more serious, and she did not look away.
“No,” she answered at once. “He didn’t say he had come for your opinion. But when he told me about the proposal, he naturally expected me to pass it on.”
Her husband gave no answer.

“I was afraid you might object. Still, someone with so much ability could be very useful to my uncle, and help him do good more effectively. Mr. Ladislaw wants settled employment. He says people have criticized him for not looking for it. He’d prefer to stay here because nobody cares for him anywhere else.”

Dorothea thought that last consideration would soften her husband. When he still said nothing, she returned to Dr. Spanning and breakfast at the Archdeacon’s. Those subjects, however, had lost their sunshine.
Without telling Dorothea, Mr. Casaubon sent the following letter next morning. It began “Dear Mr. Ladislaw,” although previously he had always written “Will”—

“Mrs. Casaubon tells me you have received a proposal which, by no excessive stretch of inference, you have entertained to some degree. It would entail your residing in this neighborhood in a capacity affecting my own position. Considered in the light of my legitimate feelings, that effect makes my objection natural and justified; considered in the light of my responsibilities, it makes stating that objection a duty. I therefore inform you at once that accepting this proposal would be highly offensive to me. No reasonable person acquainted with our relationship would, I believe, deny that I have some right of veto here. Your recent conduct has relegated that relationship to the past, but cannot erase its force as a determining antecedent. I do not propose to comment on anyone’s judgment. I need only remind you that social fitness and propriety should prevent a fairly close relation of mine from becoming conspicuous in this vicinity in a position not only greatly inferior to my own, but associated at best with the superficial learning of literary or political adventurers. In any event, should you proceed otherwise, you can no longer be received at my house.
Yours faithfully, “EDWARD CASAUBON.”

Meanwhile Dorothea’s thoughts were innocently preparing to embitter her husband further. She dwelt with a sympathy growing into agitation on Will’s account of his parents and grandparents. She usually spent her private hours in the blue-green boudoir and had become fond of its pale quaintness. Nothing in its outward appearance had changed. But as summer gradually spread over the western fields beyond the elm avenue, the bare room had accumulated memories of her inner life. These filled the air like a cloud of good or bad angels, invisible but active forms of spiritual victories and defeats. So often had she struggled for resolution and found it while looking down the avenue toward the arch of western light that the view itself now seemed able to speak to her. Even the pale stag appeared to exchange remembering glances and silently say, “Yes, we know.” The finely painted miniatures formed an audience of beings no longer troubled about their own earthly fates but retaining a human concern for others. Especially the mysterious “Aunt Julia,” about whom she had always found it difficult to question her husband.

Since talking to Will, fresh images had gathered around this Aunt Julia, his grandmother. The presence of the delicate miniature, so like a living face she knew, concentrated her feelings. How wrong to deprive a girl of family protection and inheritance merely for choosing a poor man! As a child, Dorothea had troubled her elders with questions about the world around her. She had worked her way to some independent understanding of the historical and political arguments for eldest sons’ superior rights and for keeping land under entail. Those arguments inspired a certain awe and might carry more weight than she understood. But these family ties did not challenge them. Here was a daughter whose child would have had a prior claim even under the usual imitation of aristocratic arrangements by people no grander than retired grocers, with no more land to “keep together” than a lawn and paddock. Did inheritance depend on personal liking or on responsibility? Every force in Dorothea’s nature sided with responsibility: honoring claims created by our own actions, such as marrying and becoming parents.

Mr. Casaubon truly owed the Ladislaws a debt, she told herself. He must restore what they had unjustly lost. She began thinking about the will he had made when they married, leaving most of his property to her with provisions for possible children. It ought to be changed without delay. The question of Will’s employment, newly raised, offered a chance to put matters on a fresh and just basis. Everything her husband had done before assured her that he would accept the fair view if she proposed it—she, for whose benefit this unfair concentration of property had been arranged. His sense of justice had overcome, and would continue to overcome, anything that might be called personal aversion. She suspected that he disapproved of her uncle’s plan. That made a new understanding still more timely. Instead of beginning penniless and taking the first position offered, Will should receive the income rightfully his, paid by her husband during his lifetime and secured after his death by an immediate change to the will. Seeing this as their duty felt like daylight suddenly entering, waking Dorothea from her former dull, incurious absorption in herself and ignorance of her husband’s obligations to others. Will had rejected further assistance for a reason she no longer thought sound. Mr. Casaubon himself had never fully recognized the claim on him. “But he will!” she said. “That’s where the great strength of his character lies. And what use are we making of our money? We don’t use half our income. My own fortune buys nothing but a troubled conscience.”

Dividing property set aside for herself, which she had always considered excessive, held a particular fascination for Dorothea. She was blind, you see, to much that others plainly saw, and liable, as Celia had warned, to step in the wrong places. Yet her blindness to anything outside her pure intention led her safely beside precipices where clear sight might have made her dangerously afraid.

The thoughts that had grown vivid in her quiet boudoir occupied her throughout the day on which Mr. Casaubon sent his letter. Everything felt like an obstacle until she could find a chance to speak openly to him. His absorbed mind required every subject to be approached gently. Since his illness, she had never forgotten the fear of upsetting him. Yet when youthful ardor broods over the idea of an immediate action, the action itself seems to spring into independent life and overcome obstacles in imagination. The day passed gloomily, as days often did, though her husband was perhaps quieter than usual. Night, however, offered hours when conversation might be possible. Whenever she knew he was wakeful, Dorothea had formed the habit of getting up, lighting a candle, and reading him back to sleep. This night her resolutions kept her awake from the beginning. He slept his usual few hours. She had already risen softly and sat in the darkness for nearly an hour when he spoke—
“Dorothea, as you’re already up, would you light a candle?”
“Are you unwell, dear?” she asked first, doing as he requested.
“Not at all. But since you’re awake, I would be grateful for a few pages of Lowth.”
“Could I talk to you instead, just for a little while?” Dorothea asked.
“Of course.”
“I’ve been thinking about money all day. I’ve always had too much, especially too much to look forward to.”
“Such arrangements, my dear Dorothea, are made by Providence.”
“But when we have too much because someone else has been wronged, surely we must obey the divine voice telling us to put it right.”
“What are you referring to, my love?”
“You’ve made arrangements too generous to me—I mean concerning property—and they make me unhappy.”
“Why should they? My other relations are all comparatively distant.”

“I’ve been thinking about your aunt Julia. She was left poor only because she married a poor man. That wasn’t disgraceful, since he wasn’t unworthy. I know that was why you educated Mr. Ladislaw and supported his mother.”
Dorothea paused, hoping an answer would help her continue. None came. Her next words felt all the more forceful as they fell distinctly into the dark silence.

“But surely his claim is much greater than that, even to half the property you’ve arranged to leave me. I believe we ought to provide for him immediately on that basis. It can’t be right for him to remain dependent and poor while we’re wealthy. And if there are objections to the offer he mentioned, giving him his proper position and share would remove any reason for him to accept it.”
“Mr. Ladislaw has presumably discussed this subject with you?” Mr. Casaubon asked with an uncharacteristic, biting quickness.

“Certainly not!” Dorothea answered earnestly. “How can you think that, when he so recently refused everything you offered? I’m afraid you’re too harsh in your judgment of him, dear. He merely told me a little about his parents and grandparents, mostly because I asked. You’ve been so good and just. You’ve done everything you believed right. But I can plainly see that justice requires more. I have to speak because I’m the one who would receive what people call the benefit if that further duty were left undone.”
There was a noticeable pause before Mr. Casaubon answered. He no longer spoke quickly, but his emphasis cut still more deeply.

“Dorothea, my love, this is not the first time you have presumed to judge subjects beyond your understanding. It would be well if it were the last. I shall not now discuss how far a person’s conduct, especially in marriage, may forfeit claims on a family. It is enough to say that you are not qualified to judge the matter. What I require you to understand is that I accept no revision of my decisions, still less direction, in affairs I have considered distinctly and properly my own. You must not interfere between Mr. Ladislaw and me. Still less should you encourage communications from him which amount to criticism of my conduct.”

Hidden in the darkness, poor Dorothea was overwhelmed by conflicting feelings. Fear of what her husband’s fierce anger might do to his health would have silenced her own resentment, even had she felt no doubt or remorse at the possibility of some truth in his final insinuation. She heard him breathing rapidly after speaking and sat listening, frightened and miserable. Silently she cried for help to endure this nightmare existence in which fear arrested every impulse to act. Nothing further happened. They simply lay awake a long time, neither speaking again.
The following day Mr. Casaubon received this reply from Will Ladislaw—

“DEAR MR. CASAUBON,—I have considered yesterday’s letter carefully, but cannot entirely share your understanding of our relationship. I fully acknowledge your past generosity. Nevertheless, an obligation of that kind cannot justly restrict me in the way you appear to expect. Even granting that a benefactor’s wishes carry some claim, the nature of those wishes must always be considered. They may conflict with more pressing duties. Or his prohibition might empty a man’s life so completely that the resulting deprivation would be crueler than the original benefit was generous. I offer these merely as forceful illustrations. In this particular case, I cannot agree with your account of how my accepting employment—certainly not lucrative, but not dishonorable either—would affect your own standing. Your position seems far too substantial to be influenced in such an insubstantial fashion. I do not believe any change in our relations will cancel the obligations imposed by the past; certainly no such change has yet occurred. But forgive me if I cannot see why those obligations should prevent my exercising the ordinary freedom to live where I please and support myself in any lawful employment I choose. I regret our disagreement about a relationship in which all the benefits have come from you.
I remain yours, under a continuing obligation, WILL LADISLAW.”

Poor Mr. Casaubon believed no man ever had better grounds for disgust and suspicion. Must not we, in fairness, sympathize with him a little? He was certain young Ladislaw meant to defy and distress him, to capture Dorothea’s trust and plant disrespect, perhaps even aversion, toward her husband in her mind. Some concealed motive had been needed to explain Will’s abrupt change of direction in refusing further help and abandoning his travels. His defiant resolve to settle nearby by undertaking Mr. Brooke’s Middlemarch schemes, so unlike his former choice of occupation, now revealed clearly enough that Dorothea was the hidden motive. Mr. Casaubon never for an instant suspected her of deceit. He had no suspicions about her. Instead, scarcely more comfortably, he knew she was inclined to judge her husband’s conduct while looking favorably on Will and letting his words influence her. His own proud silence had prevented anyone correcting his belief that she had originally persuaded her uncle to invite Will to the Grange.

On receiving Will’s reply, Mr. Casaubon had to decide his duty. He could never comfortably have called his intended action anything else. Here, however, competing motives drove him back toward doing nothing.

Should he approach Mr. Brooke directly and require that troublesome gentleman to withdraw the offer? Or consult Sir James Chettam and persuade him to join a protest against something affecting the entire family? Either way, failure seemed as likely as success. He could not possibly mention Dorothea in this connection. Without some alarming pressure, Mr. Brooke might listen to every argument in apparent agreement, then finish with, “Don’t worry, Mr. Casaubon! You can depend on young Ladislaw doing you credit. I’ve found exactly the right thing for him, depend upon it.” Nor could Mr. Casaubon contemplate a conversation with Sir James without nervous reluctance. There had never been warmth between them, and Sir James would immediately think of Dorothea whether her name was spoken or not.

Poor Mr. Casaubon distrusted everyone’s feelings about him, especially as a husband. Allowing them to suppose him jealous would concede their suspected opinion of his disadvantages. Letting them discover that married life had not made him particularly happy would suggest he now shared their probable earlier disapproval. It would be as bad as letting Carp, and Brasenose generally, learn how far behind he was in arranging the materials for his “Key to all Mythologies.” Throughout his life he had tried to conceal, even from himself, the inward wounds of self-doubt and jealousy. On this most delicate of personal subjects, his habit of proud, suspicious reserve carried double weight.
So Mr. Casaubon kept his proud, bitter silence. But he had barred Will from Lowick Manor, and in his mind he was preparing other means of frustrating him.
